stimuli.text: Researchers want to investigate whether a brief mindfulness exercise before tests improves scores. They have 80 students in a statistics class available.

Random samples of 15 were taken from two groups. The values of commute time (minutes) are:

**City A:** 12, 15, 15, 17, 19, 19, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 27, 27, 29, 30

**City B:** 16, 21, 22, 30, 31, 32, 33, 36, 37, 41, 43, 43, 45, 45, 74

A random sample of 29 students at a large school reported hours of sleep on a school night: x̄ = 7.76 hours, s = 1.26 hours. A dotplot of the data shows no strong skew or outliers. A health report claims students at the school sleep 7 hours on average.

Data were collected on outdoor temperature (°F) (x) and daily iced-drink sales (y) for a sample of days. A scatterplot shows a linear pattern, and the residual plot shows no pattern. Computer output for the least-squares regression is shown.

```text
Predictor   Coef      SE Coef
Constant    50.1
x           2.5
S = 2    R-Sq = 80.0%
```

questions.stem: For a distribution of home prices in a county, the mean is 41 and the median is 54. Which is the most likely shape?

options.why: A uniform distribution is symmetric, with mean near the median.
The mean is pulled toward the tail.
In a symmetric distribution, the mean and median are close.
Correct. A long left tail pulls the mean below the median.

questions.explanation: Mean 41 < median 54: the mean is pulled toward the left tail.

questions.stem: The slope of a regression line predicting exam score from hours studied is 3.5. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: For each additional hour studied, the predicted exam score increases by about 3.5 points
options.why: Correct. Slope is the predicted change in y per unit of x.

options.text: Each student's score increases by exactly 3.5 points per hour
options.why: The slope describes predicted, not actual, values.

options.text: 35% of the variation in scores is explained
options.why: That is r².

options.text: A student who studies 0 hours scores 3.5
options.why: That would be the intercept.

questions.explanation: Slope is the predicted change in y per unit of x.

questions.stem: In a random sample of 300 teenagers in a state, 123 get at least 8 hours of sleep. Which is a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all teenagers in a state who get at least 8 hours of sleep?

options.why: Use the standard error, √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).
Multiply the standard error by z*.
Correct. p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) with z* = 1.96.
Divide by n inside the square root.

questions.stem: P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.6 and P(A and B) = 0.09. What is P(A or B), and are A and B independent?

options.why: Subtract P(A and B) so the overlap is not counted twice.
Correct. P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); independent if P(A and B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.18.
P(A and B) is not 0, so they are not mutually exclusive.
Compare P(A and B) with P(A)·P(B) = 0.18.

questions.stem: Two independent random samples have n₁ = 52, s₁ = 11 and n₂ = 21, s₂ = 11. What is the standard error of x̄₁ − x̄₂?

options.why: Add variances, then take the square root; standard errors do not add.
Correct. √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).
Variances add, even for a difference.
Each sample contributes s²/n.

questions.stem: A radio station asks listeners to call in with their opinions about a new law. Which type of bias is most likely?

options.text: No bias, because listeners chose freely
options.why: Self-selection causes bias.
The question wording is not the main issue.
Correct. People with strong opinions are more likely to call.
The main problem is self-selection.

questions.explanation: People with strong opinions are more likely to call.

questions.stem: What is the expected value of X?

options.why: That is the most likely value (mode), not the mean.
Correct. μ = Σ x·P(x).
Weight each value by its probability.
That is the largest probability, not the mean.

questions.stem: The correlation between temperature and ice cream sales is r = 0.7. Which is a correct interpretation of r²?

options.text: About 70% of the variation in ice cream sales is accounted for by the model
options.why: Square r.

options.text: About 49% of the variation in ice cream sales is accounted for by the linear model relating ice cream sales to temperature
options.why: Correct. r² is the proportion of variation in y explained by the linear model.

options.text: Temperature causes 49% of ice cream sales
options.why: Regression does not establish causation.

options.text: About 49% of the predictions are correct
options.why: r² is about variation explained, not accuracy of individual predictions.

questions.stem: In a random sample of 570 customers of an online store, 171 would recommend it to a friend. Which is a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all customers of an online store who would recommend it to a friend?

options.why: Use the standard error, √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).
Correct. p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) with z* = 1.96.
Divide by n inside the square root.
Multiply the standard error by z*.

questions.stem: The regression line is ŷ = 19 − 1.9x. An observation has x = 17 and y = -18. What is its residual, and what does it mean?

options.text: -4.7; the actual value is below the predicted value
options.why: Correct. Residual = y − ŷ.
That is the predicted value ŷ.

options.text: -4.7; the actual value is above the predicted value
options.why: A positive residual means the point is above the line.

options.text: 4.7; the actual value is above the predicted value
options.why: Residual = actual − predicted, not predicted − actual.

questions.stem: A student is chosen at random from those who drive to school. What is the probability the student is a junior?

options.why: That is P(junior and drives); divide by drivers only.
That is P(drives | junior).
That is P(junior) overall.
Correct. P(junior | drives) = juniors who drive ÷ all who drive.

questions.stem: A sample of 12 values is used for a one-sample t interval. Which condition must be checked because the sample is small?

options.text: The sample size is at least 30
options.why: That is the large-sample alternative.
That is for proportions.

options.text: The sample data show no strong skewness or outliers (population approximately normal)
options.why: Correct. Small samples need approximate normality.
That is for chi-square tests.

questions.stem: For a distribution of household incomes in a city, the mean is 63 and the median is 70. Which is the most likely shape?

options.why: A uniform distribution is symmetric, with mean near the median.
The mean is pulled toward the tail.
In a symmetric distribution, the mean and median are close.
Correct. A long left tail pulls the mean below the median.

questions.explanation: Mean 63 < median 70: the mean is pulled toward the left tail.

questions.stem: A principal divides students by grade level and takes a simple random sample of 25 students from each grade. What sampling method is this?

options.why: Correct. SRSs within groups (strata).
That selects every kth individual.
The selection is random.
Cluster sampling selects whole groups.

questions.stem: Each of 8 independent devices fails with probability 0.1. What is the probability that at least one fails?

options.why: Probabilities of overlapping events cannot simply be added.
Correct. 1 − P(none fail) = 1 − (1 − p)^n.
That is the probability none fail.
That is the probability all fail.

questions.stem: Which variable is quantitative?

options.text: Whether a student owns a car (yes or no)
options.why: That is categorical.
Zip codes are labels.
That is categorical.

options.text: The number of text messages a student sends per day
options.why: Correct. Counts are quantitative.

questions.stem: Two independent random samples have n₁ = 54, s₁ = 12 and n₂ = 59, s₂ = 18. What is the standard error of x̄₁ − x̄₂?

options.why: Each sample contributes s²/n.
Correct. √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).
Add variances, then take the square root; standard errors do not add.
Variances add, even for a difference.

questions.stem: The data are: 11, 13, 15, 21, 22, 22, 25, 29, 59. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, which statement is correct?

options.text: There are no outliers because every value is within 2 standard deviations of the mean
options.why: The 1.5 × IQR rule is the method asked for.

options.text: Q1 = 14, Q3 = 27; values above 41.5 are outliers
options.why: Add 1.5·IQR to Q3, not to the median.

options.text: Q1 = 14, Q3 = 27; values above 40 are outliers, so 59 is an outlier
options.why: The fence uses 1.5 × IQR, not 1 × IQR.

options.text: Q1 = 14, Q3 = 27; values above 46.5 are outliers, so 59 is an outlier
options.why: Correct. IQR = 13; upper fence = Q3 + 1.5·IQR = 46.5.

questions.stem: Each of 13 independent trials succeeds with probability 0.7. What is the probability of at most 9 successes?

options.why: That is only P(X = k).
That is the complement.
That is P(X < k); 'at most k' includes k.
Correct. Use the binomial distribution with n = 13 and p = 0.7.

questions.stem: A test of H₀: p = 0.4 versus Hₐ: p > 0.4 gives a p-value of 0.03. Which interpretation is correct?

options.why: Unrelated to the p-value.

options.text: If p = 0.4, there is a 0.03 probability of a sample proportion at least as large as the one observed, by chance alone
options.why: Correct. That is the definition of the p-value.

options.text: There is a 0.97 probability that Hₐ is true
options.why: Not a valid interpretation.

options.text: There is a 0.03 probability that H₀ is true
options.why: A p-value is not the probability of a hypothesis.

questions.explanation: That is the definition of the p-value.

questions.stem: A random sample of 17 gives x̄ = 200.2 and s = 7. Test H₀: μ = 198 versus Hₐ: μ > 198. What are the test statistic and p-value?

options.why: Divide by the standard error s/√n.
Use the t distribution, not the normal.
The alternative is one-sided.
Correct. t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) with df = n − 1.

questions.stem: For a set of data, x̄ = 13, sx = 2, ȳ = 46, sy = 22 and r = 0.5. What is the least-squares regression line?

options.why: a = ȳ − b·x̄.
Multiply sy/sx by r.
The slope is r·sy/sx, not r·sx/sy.
Correct. b = r·sy/sx and a = ȳ − b·x̄.

questions.stem: A random sample of 31 has mean 43.6 and standard deviation 14.4. Which is a 95% confidence interval for the population mean?

options.why: Correct. x̄ ± t*·s/√n with t* = 2.042 (df = 30).
With s estimating σ, use t*, not z*.
Divide s by √n.
Divide by √n, not n.

questions.stem: X and Y are independent with μX = 35, σX = 5, μY = 18, σY = 3. What are the mean and standard deviation of X − Y?

options.why: Check the sign of the mean.
That is the variance; take the square root.
Standard deviations do not add; variances do.
Correct. Means add or subtract; variances add.

questions.stem: To test H₀: p = 0.7 versus Hₐ: p > 0.7, a random sample of 180 gives p̂ = 0.76. What are the test statistic and p-value?

options.why: Correct. z = (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀(1 − p₀)/n); one-sided p-value.
The alternative is one-sided.
The test's standard deviation uses p₀, not p̂.
Find the area in the direction of Hₐ.

questions.stem: A population has mean 82 and standard deviation 15 (shape unknown). For random samples of 64, what is the approximate probability that the sample mean exceeds 84.3?

options.why: That is the area below.
Use σ/√n for a sample mean.
Correct. By the CLT, x̄ is approximately normal with SD 15/√64 = 1.875.
Divide σ by √n, not n.

questions.stem: A random sample of 26 has mean 40.7 and standard deviation 8.2. Which is a 95% confidence interval for the population mean?

options.why: Divide by √n, not n.
Divide s by √n.
With s estimating σ, use t*, not z*.
Correct. x̄ ± t*·s/√n with t* = 2.06 (df = 25).

questions.stem: To test H₀: p = 0.2 versus Hₐ: p < 0.2, a random sample of 220 gives p̂ = 0.15. What are the test statistic and p-value?

options.why: The alternative is one-sided.
Correct. z = (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀(1 − p₀)/n); one-sided p-value.
The test's standard deviation uses p₀, not p̂.
Find the area in the direction of Hₐ.

questions.stem: A random sample of 32 gives x̄ = 52.9 and s = 12. Test H₀: μ = 51 versus Hₐ: μ > 51. What are the test statistic and p-value?

options.why: The alternative is one-sided.
Use the t distribution, not the normal.
Divide by the standard error s/√n.
Correct. t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) with df = n − 1.

questions.stem: Which graph is appropriate for displaying the distribution of favorite music genres among students?

options.why: Histograms are for quantitative data.
Scatterplots need two quantitative variables.
Boxplots are for quantitative data.
Correct. Genre is categorical.

questions.stem: The data are: 14, 14, 20, 21, 25, 26, 27, 29, 32, 34, 37, 55. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, which statement is correct?

options.text: Q1 = 20.5, Q3 = 33; values above 45.3 are outliers
options.why: Add 1.5·IQR to Q3, not to the median.

options.text: Q1 = 20.5, Q3 = 33; values above 51.8 are outliers, so 55 is an outlier
options.why: Correct. IQR = 12.5; upper fence = Q3 + 1.5·IQR = 51.8.

options.text: Q1 = 20.5, Q3 = 33; values above 45.5 are outliers, so 55 is an outlier
options.why: The fence uses 1.5 × IQR, not 1 × IQR.

options.text: There are no outliers because every value is within 2 standard deviations of the mean
options.why: The 1.5 × IQR rule is the method asked for.

questions.stem: A student is chosen at random from those who drive to school. What is the probability the student is a junior?

options.why: That is P(junior) overall.
That is P(drives | junior).
That is P(junior and drives); divide by drivers only.
Correct. P(junior | drives) = juniors who drive ÷ all who drive.

questions.stem: Why does an experiment use random assignment?

options.text: To guarantee a large sample size
options.why: Randomization does not affect size.

options.text: To create treatment groups that are roughly equivalent, so differences in response can be attributed to the treatments
options.why: Correct. Randomization balances other variables.
Blinding is separate.

options.text: To allow generalization to a larger population
options.why: That requires random selection.

questions.stem: A variable is approximately normal with mean 106 and standard deviation 17. What value is at the 80th percentile?

options.why: Correct. z = invNorm(0.8) ≈ 0.842; x = μ + zσ.
Use the z-score for the percentile, not the percentile itself.
Check the sign of z.
Multiply z by σ, not σ².

questions.stem: What is the smallest sample size needed to estimate a proportion with a margin of error of at most 0.05 at 99% confidence, with no prior estimate of p?

options.why: Correct. n ≥ (z*/m)²(0.5)(0.5) with z* = 2.576, rounded up.
Multiply by p̂(1 − p̂) = 0.25.
Always round up to guarantee the margin.
Square z*/m.

questions.stem: Researchers randomly selected 200 adults in the state and randomly assigned them to use one of two study apps, then compared test scores. Can the researchers conclude that the app causes higher scores, and to whom do the results apply?

options.text: Yes to cause and effect, but only for the volunteers in the study
options.why: Random assignment allows causal conclusions; random selection allows generalization to the population.

options.text: Yes to cause and effect, and yes to generalizing to all adults in the state
options.why: Correct. Random assignment decides causation; random selection decides generalization.

options.text: No to cause and effect, and no generalization beyond the volunteers
options.why: Random assignment allows causal conclusions; random selection allows generalization to the population.

options.text: No to cause and effect, but the association can be generalized to all adults in the state
options.why: Random assignment allows causal conclusions; random selection allows generalization to the population.

questions.explanation: Random assignment: yes. Random selection: yes.

questions.stem: To test H₀: p = 0.4 versus Hₐ: p < 0.4, a random sample of 180 gives p̂ = 0.36. What are the test statistic and p-value?

options.why: The alternative is one-sided.
Find the area in the direction of Hₐ.
Correct. z = (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀(1 − p₀)/n); one-sided p-value.
The test's standard deviation uses p₀, not p̂.

questions.stem: What is the smallest sample size needed to estimate a proportion with a margin of error of at most 0.02 at 90% confidence, with no prior estimate of p?

options.why: Square z*/m.
Multiply by p̂(1 − p̂) = 0.25.
Correct. n ≥ (z*/m)²(0.5)(0.5) with z* = 1.645, rounded up.
Always round up to guarantee the margin.

questions.stem: A random sample of 19 gives x̄ = 95.7 and s = 7. Test H₀: μ = 92 versus Hₐ: μ > 92. What are the test statistic and p-value?

options.why: Correct. t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) with df = n − 1.
The alternative is one-sided.
Use the t distribution, not the normal.
Divide by the standard error s/√n.

questions.stem: Assuming the null hypothesis of a chi-square test is true, what is the expected count for Group 1, Option A?

options.why: That is the observed count.
Expected counts depend on the row and column totals.
Correct. Expected = (row total × column total) / table total.
Divide by the table total once.

questions.stem: In a randomized experiment, 95 of 190 subjects improved with treatment 1 and 49 of 140 improved with treatment 2. For a test of H₀: p₁ − p₂ = 0, what is the test statistic?

options.why: Divide the difference by its standard error.
Correct. Pooled p̂c = 0.4364; z = (p̂₁ − p̂₂)/√(p̂c(1 − p̂c)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)).
The test uses the pooled proportion, because H₀ assumes p₁ = p₂.
Use (1/n₁ + 1/n₂).

questions.stem: In a randomized experiment, 57 of 150 subjects improved with treatment 1 and 59 of 90 improved with treatment 2. For a test of H₀: p₁ − p₂ = 0, what is the test statistic?

options.why: The test uses the pooled proportion, because H₀ assumes p₁ = p₂.
Use (1/n₁ + 1/n₂).
Correct. Pooled p̂c = 0.4833; z = (p̂₁ − p̂₂)/√(p̂c(1 − p̂c)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)).
Divide the difference by its standard error.

parts.prompt: Write an investigative question for this study, and identify the explanatory and response variables.

rubric.criterion: A clear investigative question that names the population or units and the variables.
rubric.example: "Does the mindfulness exercise lead to a better score on the next unit test than a reading break for units like these?"
Explanatory: treatment (the mindfulness exercise vs a reading break). Response: score on the next unit test.

parts.prompt: Explain why an experiment, rather than an observational study, should be used to answer the question.

rubric.criterion: Only random assignment allows a cause-and-effect conclusion; an observational study could be confounded.
rubric.example: Units that choose a treatment may differ in other ways that affect the response.

parts.prompt: Describe how to randomly assign the 80 units to the two treatments in a completely randomized design.

rubric.example: Number units 1–80; use a random number generator to select 40 different numbers.
Those 40 receive the mindfulness exercise; the remaining 40 receive a reading break.

parts.prompt: The researchers consider blocking by previous test average (high or low). Explain how blocking would be carried out and why it could improve the experiment.

rubric.criterion: Form blocks and randomize within each block.
rubric.example: Separate units into the blocks, then randomly assign half of each block to each treatment.

rubric.criterion: Benefit: reduces variability in the response due to the blocking variable, making a treatment effect easier to detect.
rubric.example: Accounts for differences caused by previous test average.

parts.prompt: Find the five-number summary for each group.
Use the 1.5 × IQR rule to determine whether City B has any outliers. Show your work.

rubric.example: IQR = 13; upper fence = 43 + 1.5(13) = 62.5. Outlier(s): 74.

parts.prompt: Compare the distributions of the two groups (shape, center and variability) in context.

rubric.example: The median for City B (36) is greater than for City A (20).
City B is more variable (IQR 13 vs 10).

rubric.criterion: Comments on shape or unusual features.
rubric.example: City B has a high outlier, suggesting right skew.

parts.prompt: Which measure of center is more appropriate for City B, the mean or the median? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Median, because it is resistant to the outlier or skew.
rubric.example: Mean 36.6 is pulled toward the high value; median 36 is not.

parts.prompt: Identify the procedure and check the conditions for a 95% confidence interval for the mean.

rubric.criterion: One-sample t interval; random, 10%, and normality justified by the dotplot (n under 30).
rubric.example: n = 29; the sample shows no strong skew or outliers.

rubric.criterion: Confidence in capturing the population mean.
rubric.example: We are 95% confident that the interval from 7.28 to 8.23 hours captures the true mean hours of sleep for students at the school.

parts.prompt: Does the interval support the report's claim? Explain.

rubric.example: 7 is outside the interval, so it is not plausible; the data contradict the claim.

parts.prompt: Write the equation of the least-squares regression line, defining the variables.

rubric.example: ŷ = 50.1 + 2.5x, where ŷ is predicted daily iced-drink sales and x is outdoor temperature (°F).

parts.prompt: Interpret the slope and the value of R-Sq in context.

rubric.example: For each additional unit of outdoor temperature (°F), the predicted daily iced-drink sales increases by about 2.5.
About 80.0% of the variation in daily iced-drink sales is accounted for by the linear model with outdoor temperature (°F).

parts.prompt: One observation has x = 4 and y = 56.1. Calculate and interpret its residual. Also find the correlation r.

rubric.example: ŷ = 60.1; residual = 56.1 − 60.1 = -4: the actual value is below the prediction.

parts.prompt: The data come from a convenience sample. Explain how this affects the conclusions and describe a better data collection method.

rubric.criterion: Results may not generalize to the population; a random sample would allow generalization.
rubric.example: Take a simple random sample of days from the population of interest. Observational data also cannot show causation.
